summary: Defines the data fields and data types for In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance, a way to record operational and telemetry information inside packets as they travel a path. The fields can be carried in several encapsulations, such as NSH, Segment Routing, Geneve, or IPv6. It complements probe-based tools like ICMP. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) records information about a packet as it travels through a managed network domain. This RFC defines the information fields, while separate specifications define how protocols carry them.

subtitle: Fields for recording operational data as packets cross a managed network domain.

tldr.problem: Probe packets can be handled differently from ordinary traffic, so their results may not describe the path taken by data packets.
tldr.mechanism: IOAM defines fields that edge and transit nodes place in or update on packets inside a limited domain. Separate specifications define how each network protocol carries those fields.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines four option types and their data fields, but not an encapsulation. Any specification that carries these fields MUST provide cryptographic integrity protection.

today: RFC 9197 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2022. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; encapsulation details are left to separate specifications.

sections.title: What IOAM Records
sections.content:
In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) adds operational information to packets that already carry user traffic. Nodes along the path can record details such as their identity, interfaces, timestamps, and transit delay.

This approach complements probe-based tools such as Ping and Traceroute. It can show whether a flow followed a defined path or how ordinary traffic was distributed across paths, including cases where probes receive different treatment.
sections.plainLanguage: IOAM records information in packets that already carry data. The records can show which nodes handled a packet and how it moved through them.

sections.title: Scope and Limited Domains
sections.content:
This RFC defines IOAM data fields and their types. It does not define how to carry them in Network Service Header, Segment Routing, Geneve, IPv6, or another encapsulation; each carrying protocol needs its own specification.

IOAM is intended for limited domains, such as a campus or an overlay network. Operators are expected to prevent IOAM data from crossing the domain boundary, and SHOULD consider larger packet sizes, path MTU, and effects on load balancing.

An operator may apply IOAM to all traffic or only selected traffic. When tunnels stack, each layer's IOAM data operates independently of the data at other layers.
sections.plainLanguage: IOAM is designed for a managed network domain, not for unrestricted passage across the Internet. Operators need to keep its data inside the domain and allow for the extra packet size.

sections.title: Node Roles and Namespaces
sections.content:
An encapsulating node adds IOAM options, a decapsulating node removes them, and a transit node reads or updates data while forwarding a packet. A transit node MUST ignore option types it does not understand and MUST NOT add or remove options.

Each option carries a 16-bit Namespace-ID. The value 0x0000 is the default and MUST be supported; 0x0001 through 0x7FFF are operator-assigned, while 0x8000 through 0xFFFF are assigned by IANA. A node that is not configured for a packet's namespace MUST NOT change its IOAM fields.

A namespace gives data context. For example, node identifiers need only be unique within the namespace, and the namespace can define how a timestamp or unitless field is interpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node has a role: add the IOAM data, update it while forwarding, or remove it at the domain edge. The Namespace-ID tells a node which data it is configured to handle.

sections.title: The Two Trace Option Formats
sections.content:
The Pre-allocated Trace Option reserves room for node records before a packet enters the domain. Each transit node fills its assigned space, beginning at the last array entry and working backward.

The Incremental Trace Option lets each node add its record after the option header. Encapsulating and decapsulating nodes that support tracing MUST support both formats; a transit node needs to support only one. When both appear, the Incremental option MUST come first.

The shared header carries the namespace, per-node record length, flags, remaining space, a 24-bit Trace-Type bit field, and reserved bits. If there is not enough room, a node adds no fields and sets the overflow flag.
sections.plainLanguage: IOAM offers two ways to store a trace: reserve space for all nodes in advance, or let each node add its record. The Trace-Type identifies which fields each record contains.

sections.title: Fields in Each Node Record
sections.content:
The Trace-Type selects the fields in each node record, which are packed in bit order and aligned to four octets. Defined fields include node and interface identifiers, timestamp seconds and fraction, transit delay, namespace-specific data, queue depth, buffer occupancy, and a checksum complement.

Several identifiers have short four-octet and wide eight-octet formats. If a node cannot fill a requested field, it uses an all-ones value to mean that the field was not populated. Queue and buffer measurements can use implementation-specific units, interpreted in the namespace context.

The optional Opaque State Snapshot is variable length. Its 24-bit Schema ID selects a schema known to the analyzer through a mechanism outside this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: A trace record can identify a node, its interfaces, packet timing, and selected node measurements. If a node cannot provide a requested value, it marks that field as not populated.

sections.title: Proof of Transit and Edge-to-Edge Data
sections.content:
The Proof of Transit option carries a packet identifier and a cumulative value that nodes update according to a verification algorithm. This RFC defines POT-Type 0, with a 64-bit PktID and a 64-bit Cumulative field; it does not define the verification algorithm.

The Edge-to-Edge option carries data from the encapsulating node for the decapsulating node. Transit nodes MAY process it but MUST NOT modify it. Defined data can include a 64-bit or 32-bit sequence number, but not both, and timestamps for when the packet entered the domain.

The RFC establishes seven IOAM registries. Option-Type values 0 through 3 identify the four defined options; new option types use IETF Review, while Namespace-ID values in the IANA range use Expert Review.
sections.plainLanguage: Proof of Transit carries values that a separate method can use to check a packet's route. Edge-to-Edge data is written at entry and read at exit; transit nodes cannot change it.

sections.title: Security and Data Exposure
sections.content:
Someone who changes IOAM data can hide failures or create false evidence about a packet's path. Data may also expose network paths, performance, queue state, and buffer use, especially if it leaves its IOAM domain.

Any specification that defines an IOAM encapsulation MUST provide cryptographic integrity protection for the fields. Operators are expected to restrict IOAM processing to authorized devices and prevent data from leaking across domain boundaries.

Adding IOAM fields can increase packet size enough to cause fragmentation or loss. The RFC also notes risks from resource-exhaustion attacks, altered timestamps, and maliciously changed Proof of Transit data.
sections.plainLanguage: Unprotected IOAM data can be changed or used to learn about a network. The carrying protocol must protect its integrity, and operators should keep the data within the managed domain.

fields.name: Namespace-ID
fields.desc: Identifies the namespace for interpreting the option.

fields.name: NodeLen
fields.desc: Per-node data length in four-octet units.

fields.name: RemainingLen
fields.desc: Remaining data space in four-octet units.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by the encapsulating node.

items.title: Pre-allocated Trace
items.text: Reserves node-record space before a packet enters the domain.

items.title: Incremental Trace
items.text: Each node appends its record after the option header.

items.title: Proof of Transit
items.text: Carries a packet identifier and cumulative verification value.

items.title: Edge-to-Edge
items.text: Carries data from the domain entry node to its exit node.
